claim: Nearly a third of 47 sequenced non-laboratory yeast strains carried whole or partial chromosome amplification.
source: We sequenced the genomes of 47 non-laboratory yeast strains, including wild, clinical, and industrial isolates (Supplementary file 1) and assessed the copy number of the 16 yeast chromosomes. Nearly a third of all strains carried whole (12 strains) or partial (2 strains) chromosome amplification (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by genomic sequencing data from 47 strains and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Three strains harbored multiple aneuploidies, with strain Y2189 amplifying four different chromosomes.
source: Three strains harbored multiple aneuploidies, the extreme being insect-associated strain Y2189 that amplified four different chromosomes.
evidence: Supported by genomic sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Chromosome 8 was aneuploid in five unrelated isolates.
source: Chr 8 was aneuploid in five unrelated isolates.
evidence: Supported by genomic sequencing data from the 47 strains.

claim: The higher incidence of Chr 8 amplification may reflect a higher frequency of mitotic error.
source: The higher incidence of Chr 8 amplification may reflect a higher frequency of mitotic error, since diploid mutation-accumulation (MA) lines propagated in the near-absence of selection amplify Chr 8 at a higher rate (Zhu et al., 2014).
evidence: Speculation based on cited evidence from mutation-accumulation lines.

claim: Natural aneuploid strains showed no significant growth reduction compared to closely related euploid reference strains.
source: Furthermore, natural aneuploids showed no significant growth reduction compared to closely related euploid reference strains (p = 0.19, paired T-test), although there was a slight negative correlation between growth rate and extra DNA content (R = −0.3, Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by growth rate measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There was a slight negative correlation between growth rate and extra DNA content in aneuploid strains (R = −0.3).
source: Furthermore, natural aneuploids showed no significant growth reduction compared to closely related euploid reference strains (p = 0.19, paired T-test), although there was a slight negative correlation between growth rate and extra DNA content (R = −0.3, Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of growth rate data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Aneuploid laboratory strains show extreme growth retardation.
source: This is in stark contrast to aneuploid laboratory strains, which show extreme growth retardation (Torres et al., 2007; Pavelka et al., 2010 and below).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Chromosomal amplification was stable for >200–400 generations in four interrogated wild strains.
source: We also found that chromosomal amplification was stable for >200–400 generations in four interrogated wild strains, whereas the W303 laboratory strain generally loses aneuploidy within 20 generations.
evidence: Supported by experimental passaging data.

claim: The W303 laboratory strain generally loses aneuploidy within 20 generations.
source: We also found that chromosomal amplification was stable for >200–400 generations in four interrogated wild strains, whereas the W303 laboratory strain generally loses aneuploidy within 20 generations.
evidence: Supported by experimental passaging data.

claim: Aneuploid derivatives of naturally euploid parents showed little to no growth defect.
source: To distinguish if the tolerant strains have adapted to aneuploidy or if non-W303 strains can inherently accommodate chromosome amplification, we selected aneuploid derivatives of several naturally euploid parents (see 'Materials and methods'). We found little to no growth defect in derived aneuploid strains (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by growth rate measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: S. cerevisiae isolates are inherently tolerant of chromosomal amplification.
source: Thus, S. cerevisiae isolates are inherently tolerant of chromosomal amplification, which is common in nature.
evidence: Inferred from growth data and aneuploidy prevalence data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Aneuploid laboratory strains show proportionately higher expression from virtually all amplified genes.
source: Laboratory strains with forced aneuploidy are extremely slow growing, regardless of the chromosome amplified (Torres et al., 2007; Pavelka et al., 2010). Transcriptomic and proteomic studies in these strains reported proportionately higher expression from virtually all amplified genes (Torres et al., 2007; Pavelka et al., 2010; Torres et al., 2010; Sheltzer et al., 2012), with a handful of exceptions recently identified at the protein level (Dephoure et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous transcriptomic and proteomic studies.

claim: Naturally aneuploid strains did not activate the environmental stress response as seen in sickly laboratory aneuploids.
source: Consistent with their near-normal growth rates, naturally aneuploid strains did not activate the environmental stress response as seen in sickly laboratory aneuploids (Torres et al., 2007; Sheltzer et al., 2012) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A and comparison to cited studies.

claim: A weak signature common to several aneuploid strains included up-regulation of 69 unamplified genes enriched for oxidoreductases.
source: However, we detected a weak signature common to several aneuploid strains, including the up-regulation of 69 unamplified genes (enriched for oxidoreductases) and reduced expression of 269 unamplified genes (strongly enriched for mitochondrial ribosomal protein (RP) genes and genes involved in respiration) in at least three of the six aneuploid strains (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A weak signature common to several aneuploid strains included reduced expression of 269 unamplified genes strongly enriched for mitochondrial ribosomal protein genes and genes involved in respiration.
source: However, we detected a weak signature common to several aneuploid strains, including the up-regulation of 69 unamplified genes (enriched for oxidoreductases) and reduced expression of 269 unamplified genes (strongly enriched for mitochondrial ribosomal protein (RP) genes and genes involved in respiration) in at least three of the six aneuploid strains (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Naturally aneuploid yeast with variable chromosome copy number showed no growth defect on non-fermentable carbon sources.
source: We tested the respiratory capabilities of naturally aneuploid yeast with variable chromosome copy number and found no growth defect on non-fermentable carbon sources (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by growth measurements on different carbon sources shown in Figure 3.

claim: A diploid W303 strain trisomic for Chr 12 displayed an exacerbated growth defect on non-fermentable carbon sources.
source: In contrast, a diploid W303 strain trisomic for Chr 12 ('W303_Chr12-3n') displayed an exacerbated growth defect on non-fermentable carbon sources, and we were unable to make the tetrasomic W303_Chr12-4n strain that retained its mitochondrial genome, despite numerous backcrossing attempts (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by growth measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: The authors were unable to make the tetrasomic W303_Chr12-4n strain that retained its mitochondrial genome, despite numerous backcrossing attempts.
source: In contrast, a diploid W303 strain trisomic for Chr 12 ('W303_Chr12-3n') displayed an exacerbated growth defect on non-fermentable carbon sources, and we were unable to make the tetrasomic W303_Chr12-4n strain that retained its mitochondrial genome, despite numerous backcrossing attempts (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental attempts described in the text.

claim: Differences in mitochondrial function may contribute to differences in aneuploid tolerance across strain backgrounds.
source: This suggests that differences in mitochondrial function may contribute to differences in aneuploid tolerance across strain backgrounds.
evidence: Inferred from growth defect data on non-fermentable carbon sources.

claim: Up-regulation of oxidoreductases and down-regulation of mitochondrial genes are a hallmark of Down syndrome.
source: Interestingly, up-regulation of oxidoreductases and down-regulation of mitochondrial genes are a hallmark of DS (Conti et al., 2007; Lintas et al., 2012; Helguera et al., 2013; Valenti et al., 2014) (see Discussion).
evidence: Supported by citations to Down syndrome studies.

claim: Nearly 40% of amplified genes showed lower expression per gene copy compared to the paired euploid across all strains.
source: We investigated transcript abundance relative to DNA copy for amplified genes, interrogating 2204 genes spanning eight amplified chromosomes across the six aneuploids. Across all strains, nearly 40% of amplified genes showed lower expression per gene copy compared to the paired euploid (Figure 4A, blue points, see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and DNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Amplified genes with lower-than-expected expression were enriched for genes encoding ribosomal proteins, translation factors, proteins localized to the nucleus or to mitochondria.
source: These were enriched for genes encoding RPs, translation factors, proteins localized to the nucleus or to mitochondria, and other groups (p < 1e-5, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by functional enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Amplified genes with expression proportionate to gene copy showed distinct enrichment for genes encoding proteins localized to the cytoplasm or to membranes, stress defense proteins, and kinases and transferases.
source: In contrast, amplified genes with expression proportionate to gene copy (Figure 4A, gray points) showed distinct enrichment for genes encoding proteins localized to the cytoplasm or to membranes, stress defense proteins, and kinases and transferases (p < 1e-5, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by functional enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: A subset of genes was expressed ≥1.5× higher than expected per gene copy and were enriched for genes that influence morphology.
source: A subset of genes was expressed ≥1.5× higher than expected per gene copy (Figure 4A, magenta points), and these were enriched for genes that influence morphology (p = 1e-5, see more below).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis and functional enrichment shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Roughly 11–36% of amplified genes, depending on the strain, showed lower-than-expected expression in isogenic aneuploid-euploid pairs.
source: Recapitulating the results shown above, roughly 11–36% of amplified genes, depending on the strain, showed lower-than-expected expression (Figure 4B, blue points), while 2–4% showed higher-than-expected expression (Figure 4B, magenta points).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis in isogenic strain pairs shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Few genes with lower-than-expected expression participate in the common response to chromosome amplification, suggesting a mechanism of dosage compensation.
source: Few of these genes participate in the common response to chromosome amplification, suggesting a mechanism of dosage compensation.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of gene lists from different analyses.

claim: A substantial fraction of genes in the forced YPS163 aneuploid displayed reduced expression, even though this strain had little time to adapt to the aneuploidy.
source: A substantial fraction of the genes scored in the forced YPS163 aneuploid displayed reduced expression, even though this strain had little time to adapt to the aneuploidy.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from the forced aneuploid strain.

claim: Dosage compensation is likely an inherent trait in S. cerevisiae that functions at a subset of yeast genes.
source: Thus, dosage compensation is likely an inherent trait in S. cerevisiae that functions at a subset of yeast genes.
evidence: Inferred from expression data in forced aneuploid strains with little adaptation time.

claim: In the YPS1009_Chr12 strain panel, 7% of genes showed expected mRNA increases across the strain panel and with regard to the reference strain (Class 1).
source: In the YPS1009_Chr12 strain panel, 7% of genes showed expected mRNA increases across the strain panel and with regard to the reference strain (Class 1).
evidence: Supported by MLR model classification of RNA-seq data.

claim: In the YPS1009_Chr12 strain panel, 28% of genes showed heritably reduced expression per gene copy (Class 2a).
source: In contrast, 28% of genes showed heritably reduced expression per gene copy (Class 2a) while only 1% showed heritably increased expression (Class 2b).
evidence: Supported by MLR model classification of RNA-seq data.

claim: In the YPS1009_Chr12 strain panel, nearly a third of Chr 12 genes displayed a phenotype consistent with dosage compensation (Class 3a).
source: However, nearly a third of Chr 12 genes displayed a phenotype consistent with dosage compensation (Class 3a).
evidence: Supported by MLR model classification of RNA-seq data.

claim: In the NCYC110_Chr 8 strain panel, 11% of genes displayed a phenotype consistent with dosage compensation.
source: In the NCYC110_Chr 8 strain panel, 11% of genes displayed a phenotype consistent with dosage compensation while almost half the Chr 8 genes were classified as having heritably reduced expression.
evidence: Supported by MLR model classification of RNA-seq data.

claim: In the NCYC110_Chr 8 strain panel, almost half the Chr 8 genes were classified as having heritably reduced expression.
source: In the NCYC110_Chr 8 strain panel, 11% of genes displayed a phenotype consistent with dosage compensation while almost half the Chr 8 genes were classified as having heritably reduced expression.
evidence: Supported by MLR model classification of RNA-seq data.

claim: Sixteen to 20% of duplicated genes showed amplified mRNA abundance across the strain panels or in isogenic aneuploid–euploid pairs (Class 3b).
source: Sixteen to 20% of duplicated genes showed amplified mRNA abundance across the strain panels (Class 3b) or in isogenic aneuploid–euploid pairs (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by MLR model classification and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 206 genes with amplified expression were enriched for genes important for cell morphology.
source: As a group, these 206 genes were enriched for genes important for cell morphology (p = 6e-6).
evidence: Supported by functional enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Several aneuploid strains displayed differences in flocculence or cell shape compared to euploid controls.
source: We noted that several of our aneuploid strains displayed differences in flocculence or cell shape compared to euploid controls, as previously reported for aneuploid strains (Wu et al., 2010; Tan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by observations and citations to previous studies.

claim: 245 genes subject to dosage compensation were strongly enriched for translation factors, cytosolic ribosomal proteins, ribosome biogenesis genes, iron/copper transporters, guanyl-nucleotide exchange factors, and genes encoding mitochondrial proteins.
source: As a group, these genes were strongly enriched for translation factors (p = 5e-7), cytosolic RPs (p = 1e-5), ribosome biogenesis genes (p = 1e-4), iron/copper transporters (p = 4e-5), guanyl-nucleotide exchange factors (p = 7e-4), and genes encoding mitochondrial proteins (p = 3e-5).
evidence: Supported by functional enrichment analysis of dosage-compensated genes.

claim: Of the genes with lower-than-expected expression in either the haploid YPS163_Chr8-disome or diploid T73_Chr8-4n strain, 79% showed lower-than-expected expression in the NCYC110_Chr8 strain panel.
source: Of the genes with lower-than-expected expression in either the haploid YPS163_Chr8-disome or diploid T73_Chr8-4n strain, 79% showed lower-than-expected expression in the NCYC110_Chr8 strain panel.
evidence: Supported by comparison of RNA-seq data across different Chr 8 aneuploid strains.

claim: There exist strain-specific differences in the genes that are subject to dosage compensation.
source: These results raise the possibility that there exist strain-specific differences in the genes that are subject to dosage compensation (see 'Discussion').
evidence: Inferred from differences in gene classification across strains.

claim: For ribosomal protein genes RPL15A and RPL22A, transcripts did not increase despite increasing DNA copy when cloned onto a low-copy plasmid with flanking intergenic regions.
source: When cloned onto a low-copy plasmid with flanking intergenic regions, transcripts RPL15A and RPL22A did not increase despite increasing DNA copy (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR measurements shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: The dosage response of ribosomal protein genes functions in laboratory-strain backgrounds.
source: This was true regardless of allele, ploidy or strain background, indicating that the dosage response of RP genes functions in laboratory-strain backgrounds.
evidence: Inferred from qPCR data across different strain backgrounds.

claim: The dosage response was not seen when several mitochondrial genes from Chr 12 were duplicated in isolation, since mRNA for the genes increased ∼2× when the genes were amplified.
source: In contrast, the dosage response was not seen when several mitochondrial genes from Chr 12 were duplicated in isolation, since mRNA for the genes increased ∼2× when the genes were amplified (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR measurements shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: For several mitochondrial genes that remained amplified in the mini_4n strain, the dosage effect was lost, while for other genes expression remained lower than expected.
source: For several mitochondrial genes that remained amplified in this strain, the dosage effect was lost, while for other genes expression remained lower than expected (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by microarray expression data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Expression in the W303_Chr12-3n strain was highly correlated to the YPS1009_Chr12-3n strain: for two-thirds of the Class 3a genes, expression in W303_Chr12-3n was within 10% of YPS1009_Chr12-3n values.
source: Surprisingly, however, expression in the W303_Chr12-3n strain was highly correlated to the YPS1009_Chr12-3n strain: for two-thirds of the Class 3a genes, expression in W303_Chr12-3n was within 10% of YPS1009_Chr12-3n values.
evidence: Supported by comparison of RNA-seq data between strains.

claim: The dosage compensation phenotype appeared in effect at some genes in the W303_Chr12-3n strain but was lost or obscured in the W303_Chr12-4n strain.
source: Thus the dosage compensation phenotype appeared in effect at some genes in the W303_Chr12-3n strain but was lost or obscured in the W303_Chr12-4n strain.
evidence: Inferred from expression data comparison across W303 strains.

claim: Eleven mitochondrial genes on Chr 12 showed lower-than-expected expression in the YPS1009_Chr12 panel but proportionately higher (or amplified) expression in the W303_Chr12 panel.
source: One clear exception was the group of eleven mitochondrial genes on Chr 12 that showed lower-than-expected expression in the YPS1009_Chr12 panel but proportionately higher (or amplified) expression in the W303_Chr12 panel (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data comparison shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The combined set of 245 dosage-compensated genes is enriched for genes that are deleterious in very high copy in the laboratory strain.
source: Indeed, the combined set of 245 dosage-compensated genes is enriched for genes that are deleterious in very high copy in the laboratory strain (p = 0.009, Makanae et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by comparison to published data on gene overexpression toxicity.

claim: Dosage-compensated genes showed weak enrichment for proteins in multi-subunit complexes.
source: We found weak enrichment for proteins in multi-subunit complexes (p = 0.03, Pu et al., 2009), but the significance eroded if RPs were removed from the analysis.
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis using published complex data.

claim: Dosage-compensated genes displayed slightly higher transcript abundance and higher RNA polymerase occupancy than the average gene.
source: The group of dosage-compensated genes displayed slightly higher transcript abundance and higher RNA polymerase occupancy than the average gene (Chasman et al., 2014), but the trends did not hold if genes related to translation were removed.
evidence: Supported by comparison to published RNA polymerase occupancy data.

claim: Genes subject to dosage compensation and genes affected by heritably reduced expression show higher constraint compared to all genes.
source: Genes subject to dosage compensation and genes affected by heritably reduced expression show higher constraint compared to all genes, as expected for genes that are toxic when over-expressed (Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by analysis of Vg/Vm ratios shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Dosage-compensated genes show considerably higher copy-number variation than genes that display proportionate mRNA increase upon gene amplification.
source: In fact, dosage-compensated genes show considerably higher CNV than genes that display proportionate mRNA increase upon gene amplification (p = 4e-8, Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by analysis of CNV data from 103 strains shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Genes with heritably reduced expression showed relaxed constraint in copy-number variation.
source: Somewhat surprisingly, genes with heritably reduced expression also showed relaxed constraint in CNV, which may reflect that some of these genes are dosage compensated in other strain backgrounds (see 'Discussion').
evidence: Supported by CNV analysis and speculation about gene classification.

claim: Genes subject to dosage compensation show significantly higher Bv scores compared to all genes and compared to amplified genes with proportionately higher expression.
source: Genes subject to dosage compensation show significantly higher Bv scores compared to all genes and compared to amplified genes with proportionately higher expression (p = 1.7e-4).
evidence: Supported by calculation and statistical analysis of buffering capacity scores.

claim: Genes subject to dosage-compensated expression can be buffered against copy-number variation in S. cerevisiae populations.
source: Together, these results show that genes subject to dosage-compensated expression can be buffered against CNV in S. cerevisiae populations.
evidence: Inferred from CNV and buffering capacity analyses.

claim: Strains of S. cerevisiae and Saccharomyces paradoxus from wintry climates have undergone selection to maintain freeze-thaw tolerance.
source: We and others have previously shown that strains of S. cerevisiae and Saccharomyces paradoxus from wintry climates have undergone selection to maintain freeze-thaw (FT) tolerance (Will et al., 2010; Leducq et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The AQY2 water-transporter gene underlies freeze-thaw tolerance.
source: We noted that the AQY2 water-transporter gene underlying FT tolerance (Will et al., 2010) resides on Chr 12, which is amplified in New Jersey-oak strain YPS1009_Chr12-3n.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: AQY2 escapes dosage compensation, resulting in higher AQY2 expression across the YPS1009 strain panel.
source: AQY2 escapes dosage compensation, resulting in higher AQY2 expression across the strain panel (Figure 10A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Freeze-thaw resistance improves with increasing Chr 12 copy number in YPS1009.
source: Indeed, we found that FT resistance improves with increasing Chr 12 copy number in YPS1009 (Figure 10B).
evidence: Supported by freeze-thaw survival measurements shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Chr 12 amplification is advantageous to YPS1009 in nature.
source: The strong signatures of selection that we previously observed at the AQY2 gene (Will et al., 2010) and the clear relevance of the trait suggest that Chr 12 amplification is advantageous to YPS1009 in nature.
evidence: Inferred from freeze-thaw data and cited evidence of selection at AQY2.

claim: Up to 40% of amplified genes in naturally aneuploid strains show lower-than-expected expression.
source: Our results show that up to 40% of amplified genes in naturally aneuploid strains show lower-than-expected expression.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis across multiple strains.

claim: Reduced expression of amplified genes is in part due to heritable polymorphisms that down-regulate expression from amplified genes.
source: The reduced expression is in part due to heritable polymorphisms that down-regulate expression from amplified genes, some of which may have been selected for during the adaptation to aneuploidy.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of isogenic and non-isogenic strain pairs.

claim: Reduced expression of other amplified genes—up to 30–36% in some strains—appears to be actively regulated in proportion to increased gene dosage.
source: But reduced expression of other amplified genes—up to 30–36% in some strains—appears to be actively regulated in proportion to increased gene dosage.
evidence: Supported by MLR model classification of RNA-seq data from isogenic strain panels.

claim: The prevalence of dosage compensation found in yeast is likely true for other species and may explain the lack of expression increase previously noted for amplified autosomal genes in Drosophila and humans.
source: The prevalence of the dosage compensation found here is likely true for other species and may explain the lack of expression increase previously noted for amplified autosomal genes in Drosophila (Zhang et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2011) and humans (Antonarakis et al., 2004; Schuster-Bockler et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2011; Woodwark and Bateman, 2011).
evidence: Speculation based on yeast data and citations to studies in other organisms.

claim: Feedback is known to occur for several ribosomal protein genes, including excess, unassembled L32 that binds a stem loop structure in its own transcript and inhibits intron splicing, perhaps triggering mRNA degradation.
source: Feedback is known to occur for several RP genes, including excess, unassembled L32 that binds a stem loop structure in its own transcript and inhibits intron splicing, perhaps triggering mRNA degradation (Dabeva and Warner, 1987; Vilardell and Warner, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on ribosomal protein feedback.

claim: Feedback pertains more broadly to other ribosomal protein genes, including RPL15A.
source: Our results imply that feedback pertains more broadly to other RP genes, including RPL15A (Figure 7A)—notably, this transcript lacks an intron and thus must utilize a mechanism distinct from RPL32.
evidence: Inferred from qPCR data shown in Figure 7A and knowledge about RPL15A lacking an intron.

claim: Several TCA-cycle enzymes double as RNA-binding proteins that report on TCA activity.
source: For example, unassembled Cox1 protein can suppress translation of the COX1 transcript (Van Loon et al., 1983; Mick et al., 2011), while several TCA-cycle enzymes double as RNA-binding proteins that report on TCA activity (Elzinga et al., 1993; de Jong et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Natural isolates are generally tolerant to aneuploidy, whether or not they have had time to adapt to the extra chromosome.
source: Natural isolates are generally tolerant to aneuploidy, whether or not they have had time to adapt to the extra chromosome.
evidence: Supported by growth data from naturally aneuploid strains and forced aneuploid derivatives.

claim: Down syndrome cells are extremely sensitive to reactive-oxygen species and down-regulate mitochondrial respiration that in turn limits ROS production.
source: Interestingly, these trends are also seen in DS cells, which are extremely sensitive to reactive-oxygen species (ROS), and perhaps consequently, down-regulate mitochondrial respiration that in turn limits ROS production (Helguera et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Down syndrome study.

claim: Human patients display significant variability in their sensitivity to Down syndrome, suggesting genetic effects on DS pathologies.
source: Human patients display significant variability in their sensitivity to DS, suggesting genetic effects on DS pathologies (Roper and Reeves, 2006; Prandini et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Down syndrome studies.

claim: Many genes escape dosage compensation in response to aneuploidy and can contribute significantly to phenotypic variation.
source: While the expression of dosage-compensated genes is controlled in proportion to gene copy, many genes escape dosage compensation in response to aneuploidy and can contribute significantly to phenotypic variation.
evidence: Inferred from expression data showing genes with proportionate or amplified expression.

claim: Whole and partial chromosome amplification is common in laboratory selection experiments.
source: Whole and partial chromosome amplification is common in laboratory selection experiments (Dunham et al., 2002; Gresham et al., 2008; Yona et al., 2012) and is particularly prevalent in laboratory mutants that have an extreme fitness defect (Hughes et al., 2000; Koszul et al., 2004; Rancati et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to laboratory evolution studies.

claim: The Saccharomycotina karyotype is extremely stable, holding at eight or sixteen chromosomes in most pre- and post-genome duplication species, respectively.
source: Yet the Saccharomycotina karyotype is extremely stable, holding at eight or sixteen chromosomes in most pre- and post-genome duplication species, respectively.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Saccharomycotina evolution.

claim: Aneuploidy may serve as a transient intermediate that can be readily generated and readily lost depending on the selective pressures.
source: This suggests that aneuploidy may serve as a transient intermediate, one that can be readily generated—and readily lost—depending on the selective pressures.
evidence: Inferred from karyotype stability and aneuploidy prevalence data.

claim: Selection for increased stress tolerance in the laboratory produced aneuploid strains that eventually gave way to other solutions even when the selective pressure persisted.
source: Yona et al. (2012) showed that selection for increased stress tolerance in the laboratory produced aneuploid strains that eventually gave way to other solutions even when the selective pressure persisted.
evidence: Supported by citation to laboratory evolution study.

claim: Aneuploidy is frequent and tolerated in nature and may provide an important route toward natural genetic variation.
source: Our results show that aneuploidy is frequent and tolerated in nature and may provide an important route toward natural genetic variation.
evidence: Inferred from aneuploidy prevalence, tolerance, and phenotypic data.

claim: Gene duplication could provide a major force in the evolution of new gene functions by relaxing constraint on gene sequences and allowing one or both gene copies to evolve.
source: Susumu Ohno proposed over 40 years ago that gene duplication could provide a major force in the evolution of new gene functions, by relaxing constraint on gene sequences and allowing one or both gene copies to evolve (Ohno, 1970).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ohno's hypothesis.

claim: The immediate consequence of duplication is assumed to be increased expression of the affected genes.
source: The immediate consequence of duplication is assumed to be increased expression of the affected genes, and in some cases the increased expression provides a selective advantage (e.g., Sandegren and Andersson, 2009; Chang et al., 2013; Edi et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on established knowledge and citations to studies showing selective advantage.

claim: Aneuploidy is linked to myriad diseases but also facilitates organismal evolution.
source: Aneuploidy is linked to myriad diseases but also facilitates organismal evolution.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about aneuploidy.

claim: Aneuploidy comes with a fitness cost, most famously in cases of human aneuploidies such as Down syndrome.
source: However, aneuploidy comes with a fitness cost, most famously in cases of human aneuploidies such as Down syndrome (DS) (Antonarakis et al., 2004).
evidence: Based on established knowledge and citation to Down syndrome study.

claim: The reasons for aneuploidy toxicity are not entirely clear but may be due to increased expression from genes that are toxic when overexpressed.
source: The reasons for aneuploidy toxicity are not entirely clear but may be due to increased expression from genes that are toxic when overexpressed (Siegel and Amon, 2012).
evidence: Speculation supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Laboratory strains are extremely sensitive to chromosomal amplification.
source: Several studies have used Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a model for aneuploidy syndromes, since laboratory strains are extremely sensitive to chromosomal amplification.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Laboratory strains with forced aneuploidy are extremely slow growing, regardless of the chromosome amplified.
source: Laboratory strains with forced aneuploidy are extremely slow growing, regardless of the chromosome amplified (Torres et al., 2007; Pavelka et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Expression at hemizygous genes is not up-regulated to compensate for reduced gene copy.
source: The apparent lack of dosage compensation is consistent with another study by Springer et al. (2010), which found that expression at hemizygous genes is not up-regulated to compensate for reduced gene copy.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Laboratory strains have lost many features inherent in wild strains.
source: While these studies have generated important results on aneuploidy intolerance in these particular strains, one caveat is that they were all done in laboratory strains, which have lost many features inherent in wild strains (Kvitek et al., 2008; Lewis et al., 2010; Lewis and Gasch, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on laboratory vs wild strain differences.

claim: Chromosomal amplification is common in non-laboratory yeast strains.
source: Here, we report that chromosomal amplification is common in non-laboratory yeast strains, which are inherently tolerant of aneuploidy and display an active mode of gene-dosage compensation at the transcript level, for specific classes of amplified genes.
evidence: Supported by genomic sequencing data from 47 strains.

claim: Non-laboratory yeast strains are inherently tolerant of aneuploidy.
source: Here, we report that chromosomal amplification is common in non-laboratory yeast strains, which are inherently tolerant of aneuploidy and display an active mode of gene-dosage compensation at the transcript level, for specific classes of amplified genes.
evidence: Supported by growth rate data from naturally aneuploid and forced aneuploid strains.

claim: Non-laboratory yeast strains display an active mode of gene-dosage compensation at the transcript level for specific classes of amplified genes.
source: Here, we report that chromosomal amplification is common in non-laboratory yeast strains, which are inherently tolerant of aneuploidy and display an active mode of gene-dosage compensation at the transcript level, for specific classes of amplified genes.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from isogenic strain panels.

claim: Genes subject to dosage compensation are under higher expression constraint in wild populations.
